caption: Every morning for two years, Grandma's teeth were in a jelly jar by the sink. Then one morning the jar was empty, and nine weeks later she was on a ventilator.
headline: Why Grandma's jar was empty
alt_hooks:
My grandma spent eleven days in the ICU with a tube down her throat.

The respiratory therapist asked me one question. Nobody else had.

"Does she sleep in her dentures?"

I said no. I was wrong.

For two years I made one joke every morning: "Morning, Grandma's teeth."

They sat in a jelly jar by the coffee maker.

The morning the jar was empty, I should have asked why. Nine weeks later, she couldn't answer.
script:
Every morning for two years, my grandma's teeth were waiting for me in a jelly jar by the kitchen sink.

One morning in November, the jar was empty. I thought nothing of it.

Nine weeks later, she was on a ventilator. I didn't find out why that jar was empty until she could talk again.

Let me back up.

I'm Devin, twenty-seven, a line cook in Duluth, Minnesota. Two years ago I moved into Grandma's spare room.

Lorraine is eighty-six. Full dentures since nineteen eighty-eight.

That winter took three things from her.

Choir at Saint Ann's. Her eight o'clock call with her sister Marian. Pierogi Saturdays, where she pinched and I boiled.

The cough started in December. "Just a cold," she said.

Eleven dollars a month on Polident. A four-dollar brush she scrubbed with like she was sanding a deck.

Her teeth still felt slimy, so I bought a twenty-nine dollar ultrasonic cleaner online. It buzzed. The water stayed clear.

January eleventh, one a.m., I heard her breathing from the driveway. Wet. Like a straw at the bottom of a milkshake.

Aspiration pneumonia. By sunrise she had a tube down her throat in the ICU.

Night three, a respiratory therapist named Andre asked what nobody else had.

"Does she sleep in her dentures?"

No, I said. She soaks them.

The jar. Empty since November.

He explained. When you sleep, your swallow and your cough go quiet. Bits of whatever is in your mouth slide toward your lungs. Young lungs cough it up. Old lungs don't.

A denture is plastic full of tiny pores and scratches. A film of bacteria and yeast lives down in them.

Overnight, in a closed mouth, it gets eight warm hours to grow. Right at the top of the windpipe.

"Think of a kitchen sponge," he said. "Rinse it, it looks clean. Now smell it. Whatever lives in there didn't leave."

A 2015 study in the Journal of Dental Research found people eighty-five and older who slept in their dentures had more than twice the pneumonia risk over three years.

In 2016, researchers swabbed elderly hospital patients' dentures. About sixty-four percent carried pneumonia germs.

Tablets clean the surface, he said. Brushes carve new scratches. More places to hide.

Try his test tomorrow, on yours or your mom's.

Wipe the inside of the top plate with a white paper towel. Hers had soaked in Polident all night. The towel came away yellow-gray and slick.

On my break I wrote a list on a ticket pad.

One. Real ultrasonic power that reaches the pores. Two. Medical-grade UV-C light to kill what shakes loose. Three. Tap water only. Four. One button, five minutes. Five. Steel, not a toy.

One cleaner checked every line. DentalPULSE.

Forty-two thousand vibrations a second. In a ninety-day lab test of seven leading ultrasonic cleaners, six left live bacteria behind. DentalPULSE was number one.

January twenty-sixth, Grandma came home. Her teeth went in the Pod. Tap water. One button. Five minutes.

The water turned brown. Flecks spinning. From teeth that had soaked all night.

"Well, I'll be darned," she said.

Then she told me about the jar.

In November she fell in the hall at night and lay there forty minutes. Never told me.

After that she slept in her teeth. "If the paramedics come," she said, "they're not seeing me like that."

I put a motion light in the hall. We made a deal. Teeth in the Pod at nine, then into the case by her bed.

By Valentine's Day the cough was gone.

By March she was back in the altos at Saint Ann's. She calls Marian at eight again, loud enough I hear both sides.

Last Saturday we made eleven dozen pierogi. She still says I boil them wrong.

And every morning, the jelly jar by the sink is empty again.

This time, that's the good news.

If someone you love sleeps in their teeth, that film is going where their lungs are.

headline: Her doctor called it a cold
alt_hooks:
Not one doctor asked.

Not the ER. Not the ICU. Not her dentist.

My twenty-four-year-old granddaughter asked. At the funeral home.

"Grandpa. Did Gram sleep in her teeth?"

Fifty-three years married.

Twenty-eight years sleeping in our dentures. Side by side.

She died in February.

Last month I found out why. I'm still in mine.
script:
My wife's death certificate says aspiration pneumonia.

Her doctor called it a cold.

I'm seventy-seven. And I am furious.

Because the thing that killed her was in her mouth every night for twenty-eight years.

And the same thing is in mine.

Let me back up.

I'm Earl. Forty-one years at the paper mill in Bangor, Maine.

Bernadette and I were married fifty-three years.

We got full dentures the same summer, nineteen ninety-six. Called it our two-for-one.

And we both slept in them. Every night.

Nobody ever told us not to.

Mornings, side by side at the sink. Brush. Polident tablet. Eight dollars a box.

Last February she got a cough.

Doctor said a cold was going around.

Then one night she called me by her brother's name.

By morning she was in the ICU.

Four days later, she was gone.

At the funeral home, my granddaughter Kayla pulled me aside.

She's a dental hygienist. Twenty-four.

"Grandpa. Did Gram sleep in her teeth?"

Not one doctor asked. Not the ER. Not the ICU.

A twenty-four-year-old at a funeral home did.

Next morning, at my kitchen table, she explained.

A denture is plastic. Under a microscope, it's full of pores and scratches.

A slimy film of bacteria and yeast lives down in there.

Tablets fizz on the surface. Brushes scratch new grooves. The film just moves in deeper.

When you sleep, your swallow slows. Your cough goes quiet.

Drops of what's in your mouth slip into your lungs.

"You know the dishrag left balled up in the sink overnight?" she said. "How it smells in the morning?"

"That's a denture in a closed mouth for eight hours."

"And Gram was breathing it in."

Journal of Dental Research, 2015.

People eighty-five and older who slept in their dentures.

More than twice the pneumonia risk over three years.

A 2016 study swabbed the dentures of elderly hospital patients.

About two out of three had pneumonia germs living right on them.

I went in the bathroom and threw up.

Two weeks later, I started coughing.

The same cough.

I quit the Friday fish fry at the Legion hall.

I wouldn't hold my great-granddaughter, Ivy. Not with that cough.

Kayla made me do a test. Do it tonight.

Take your teeth out. Seal them in a sandwich bag. Wait ten minutes.

Open it. Smell.

I had to sit down.

That's what I'd been breathing every night.

My twenty-five dollar online ultrasonic cleaner?

It hummed. The water stayed clear.

"Grandpa, that's a jewelry cleaner," Kayla laughed.

She wrote me a list.

One. Ultrasonic strong enough to reach the pores.

Two. Medical-grade UV-C light to kill what comes loose.

Three. Tap water only. No tablets.

Four. One button. Five minutes.

Five. A steel basin.

She sent me one link.

DentalPULSE.

Forty-two thousand vibrations a second.

In a ninety-day lab test of seven leading ultrasonic cleaners, six left live bacteria.

DentalPULSE was number one.

Dentist-recommended. Rated four point eight out of five.

Kayla drove up from Portland to watch.

My teeth. Tap water. One button.

Five minutes.

The water went brown.

Brown.

From teeth I'd brushed and soaked that same morning.

Kayla didn't say anything. She just put her hand on my back.

That night I slept without my teeth for the first time in twenty-eight years.

My mouth felt naked.

I didn't care.

The cough was gone in nine days.

In June I walked back into the Legion hall on a Friday. They saved my seat.

At Ivy's baptism, I held her the whole service.

Bernadette did everything she was told.

She just wasn't told the right thing.

So I'm telling you.

headline: The cup that predicts pneumonia
alt_hooks:
Every night at ten, I collect forty sets of teeth.

The residents who won't give theirs up are the ones I see again in February.

I'd seen it for nineteen years. Then it happened to my mother.

I'm a nursing assistant. I warn families about this every winter.

The week before Thanksgiving, my own mother didn't know my name.

Aspiration pneumonia. And I knew exactly where it came from.
script:
I've worked nights in a nursing home for nineteen years. Give me one walk down the hall at ten o'clock, and I can tell you who gets pneumonia this winter.

I don't read their charts. I look at one cup.

And last year, the cup I should have checked was in my own bathroom.

Let me back up.

I'm Teresa, fifty-two, a nursing assistant in El Paso, Texas.

At ten, I collect teeth. Each resident has a cup with their name on it.

Some cups fill up. Some stay empty. Pride. Habit. A daughter who says, "Mom likes to keep them in."

The empty cups are the ones I see again in February. Coughing. Fever. Then an ambulance.

Not every time. Enough to stop calling it luck.

My mother, Amparo, is eighty-one. Full upper plate since her forties.

She slept in it. Every night. And I never once checked.

That fall took three things from her.

Seven o'clock Mass at San Judas. Sunday menudo for the whole family. And watching my grandson Mateo after school.

Dollar-store Polident, seven dollars a box. A stiff brush, scrubbed hard. My sister bought her a thirty-dollar ultrasonic thing online. It buzzed. Nothing changed.

In November she got a cough. "Allergies," she said.

The week before Thanksgiving, I came home from my shift and she didn't know my name.

Aspiration pneumonia. Five days in the hospital.

Nineteen years warning other families. I couldn't breathe.

Back at work, I cornered Joyce, our speech therapist. She runs the swallow studies.

"Why the empty cups?" I asked.

When you sleep, your swallow and your cough go quiet. A little of what's in your mouth slides into your lungs. Old lungs don't push it back out.

A denture is plastic. Under a microscope, it's full of pores and scratches. A film of bacteria and yeast lives down in them.

Overnight it grows in a closed, warm mouth, right above the airway.

"Think of the grout in your shower," she said. "Mop all you want. The black lives down in the lines."

Tablets wipe the tile. Brushes cut new lines.

She showed me a 1999 study in The Lancet.

Japanese nursing homes. With daily oral care, about eleven percent got pneumonia. Without it, nineteen. Fewer deaths, too.

And from 2015: people eighty-five and up who slept in their dentures had more than twice the pneumonia risk.

My empty cups. In a medical journal.

Try this tonight.

Run a cotton swab along the inside of the top plate. Look at the tip.

Mom's came back gray. After her Polident.

So I made a list, same as I chart.

One. Real ultrasonic power, deep enough for the pores. Two. Medical-grade UV-C light. Three. Tap water, no tablets. Four. Five minutes, one button.

Only one cleaner checked every box.

DentalPULSE.

Forty-two thousand vibrations a second. In a ninety-day lab test of seven leading ultrasonic cleaners, six left live bacteria behind. DentalPULSE was number one. Dentist-recommended. Rated four point eight out of five.

When Mom came home, her plate went in the Pod. Tap water. One button. Five minutes.

The water turned brown. Cloudy, with flecks floating.

Mom crossed herself.

Joyce came by that weekend. She held Mom's plate up to the kitchen light and said, "That's what clean looks like."

Now her plate goes in the Pod at nine, then into its case on her nightstand.

Week one, her mouth felt naked. Week two, she stopped complaining.

By Christmas the cough was gone.

In January she walked to seven o'clock Mass, holding my arm.

Sunday menudo is back. She makes too much, like always.

Every afternoon at three, Mateo runs in yelling "Abuela."

At ten o'clock, I still walk my hall and check the cups.

But the first cup I check every night is at home, before my shift.

It's steel now. And it's full.
